approach.name: one-pass hash map (value -> index)
approach.description: Single pass over nums. For each element n at index i, check whether target - n is already in the map; if so return [seen[target - n], i]. Otherwise store n -> i. The check happens before the insert, which the learner now says stops an element pairing with itself. Traced [3,3] target 6 correctly to [0,1].

Does not explain why the returned pair is valid, or trace a tricky input such as duplicates ([3,3], target 6) or negatives. Does not say why checking before inserting prevents using an element twice.
No time or extra-space cost is given, and no operations or storage are named as the cause.
Brute force is mentioned only as slower. The costs of the two approaches are not compared.

turns.learner: Brute force would scan the rest of the array for `target - n`, so that's O(n) per number and O(n²) overall. The map does a single lookup instead, which is O(1) on average, so the whole thing is O(n) with O(n) extra space for the map.

turns.learner:
At i=0, n=3, `seen` is empty so 3 isn't found, and then `seen = {3: 0}`. At i=1, n=3, `target - n = 3` is in `seen`, so it returns `[seen[3], 1]`, which is `[0, 1]`.

It works because I check the map before I store the current number, so an element can't pair with itself.
